segments.text: Hello and welcome to The Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, putting sleep in the bank, does it work? The implications of underestimating caffeine, foretelling the future through a baby's lungs, your genes in your lungs, and the value of seeing your own GP rather than just any old partner in the practice when you turn up.
Each year, an astounding 2.4 million bed days in Australian hospitals could be avoided. That's over 600,000 admissions to both public and private hospitals, and that's probably an underestimate.
At about $5,000 an admission, that's a huge amount of money, not to mention the impact on the people admitted and their families.

A British study has found that hospital admissions are reduced when people who have the kind of conditions that can result in an avoidable hospital admission regularly see the same general practitioner.
But there are barriers to this, not least being the way we pay GPs.
Elizabeth Oliver is a general practitioner who was moved to blog on what patients get
for a standard consultation fee of just over $37.
And as you hear her speak to the health report's Cathy Johnson,
think back to the last time you paid the plumber or electrician who came to your house or apartment.
So was there something that set you off that got you really mad and made you write this?
It actually was the building contractor.
I'd spent a standard consultation looking after him and doing some preventative care and talking
about prostate cancer and bowel cancer and had done this really good job of setting him up for
the next 10 years of his life in terms of his health. And he said as he walked out,
oh, that was easy money for you, wasn't it? And I kind of laughed, but it just made me think,
you've got no idea what good care you just received and how long it took me to be able
to be good enough to give that care and how much money that took. And that's in jeopardy.
So you've written this blog, What I Do for $37.05, and the government's extended freeze on GP pay
rates. What's the point that you're trying to get across? The point is that GPs are amazing value
for money. And I guess I don't know of any other profession that would accept an eight-year freeze
on an increase in their pay. And so GPs that are doing amazing work to save the healthcare system
money and to save people. And that work's been undervalued. And the more that it's undervalued,
the more that GPs get squeezed, the less time they're going to be able to spend with people
and healthcare is going to suffer as a result. And so is the budget. This isn't just about
people's care. It's also about what we can afford. We must keep people out of hospital.
We must stop people's chronic disease falling apart. We must prevent people going into psychosis.
And these are some of the things that GPs do on a daily basis. And we do that
in a very short amount of time. We're very efficient. And I think that maybe people don't
understand that this is what you get for $37.05. It's not just a complaint. It's also, isn't this
awesome? And we're not going to keep doing it for this kind of pay. What is it about a typical day
that makes you so mad about that mismatch between your reimbursement and what you do?
We see everything across the lifespan. We see sick babies. We see mums who are struggling with
postnatal depression and don't know if that's okay. And we see teenagers who are kind of
dabbling with drugs and with mental health problems. And we see old people who have seven
chronic diseases and that needs to be managed to keep them out of hospital. There's public health
stuff as well. We see people that are going overseas and might bring back hepatitis A and
put it into our food system. We do so many things that not only kind of increases people's quality
of life, but save so much money. And I think that that's really valuable. You've mentioned keeping
people out of hospital. Is that something that you feel like you often do? Often. Sometimes I
send a patient to hospital because I've gotten to the point where I can't manage them safely out of
hospital anymore. And I feel almost apologetic to the emergency department doctors for sending
that patient to hospital, but they have to go. But then in the back of my mind, I think, do you know
what? There were five others today that I could have sent and I didn't because I managed it myself.
You know, the kid with asthma kept an eye on them in the waiting room for an hour and now they're
looking a bit better so they can go home. I did that for $37. That could have been seen in an
emergency department and cost hundreds and hundreds of dollars. So yeah, I definitely think
that GPs do an incredible job and they could be doing a better job if they had a bit more time
and a bit more money. So it's really time. You're feeling squeezed for time? Yeah, absolutely.
Sometimes the problem can be solved in, say, eight minutes and that's great. But sometimes it
requires much more than that. And sometimes the patient themselves doesn't even know the scope or
the danger of the problem that they're coming in with. I'm not going to keep doing this. I'm going
to stop doing it if it stays like this. I'm a good doctor. I have patients tell me that I'm a great
doctor, but I'm not going to keep doing it for this amount of pay. And for the drain and the
toll that it takes on my life, I can't. I can't keep bulk billing. And I can't continue to deliver
good care in that way either. It's just not viable. I spent a huge amount of time and effort
and tears and blood and money to become a doctor. And I'm really proud to be one. And I know that
it's a fantastic privilege and I love my job, but I physically and mentally can't keep doing this
under these bulk billing arrangements. And with this Medicare freeze, GPs need help.
General Practitioner Elizabeth Oliver talking to Cathy Johnson.
Clare Jackson is Professor of General Practice at the University of Queensland
and heavily involved in reforms to general practice currently being mooted by the federal government.
Clare's in our Brisbane studio. Welcome to the Health Report, Clare.
Thank you very much, Norman. Pleasure to be here.
I take it you've heard this is not news to you, what you heard Elizabeth just talking about.
No, I think she's nailed many of the issues that have been circulating in the lay press
and also within the profession for a very long time,
not just here in Australia but internationally.
Over the 35 years I've been in general practice,
there's been a seismic shift in the complexity of the care that we deliver
and the need to have a lot more community resources,
both health and social care,
available for general practitioners to work with.
The business case that we are working under at the moment is 35 years old
And as it is internationally, it needs to change in this country.
And the Council of Australian Governments in April signalled a very big change the way general practice is delivered and funded in this country, starting with the health care home trials in July 1.

We'll come to that in a moment because Elizabeth thinks, well, I don't know if she does think, but I mean, she implies that the solution is she goes from $37 to some other figure that's higher than that.
But I mean, going to $42, for example, is not going to solve Elizabeth's problem.
Probably not even going to $70 solves Elizabeth's problem.
So what is this healthcare home and how will it get over this problem,
which is that you're charged peace rates for what's needed?
I mean, this trial in Britain showed the same GP looking after you,
continuity of care when you've got complex chronic problems keeps you out of hospital.
And that's absolutely the experience not only in the UK but in the US and here in Australia.
So the move is to really try and build that continuity between a patient and a preferred
provider is the term used in the US and also here in Australia. The National Health and Hospital
Reform Commission in 2009 first signalled this and we are now looking at a different model
of care for patients with complex chronic disease.
The healthcare home...
So just to be specific, this is people with heart failure,
diabetes with complications, chronic obstructive lung disease,
that sort of thing.
The papers describe it as the 10% of Australians
who require 50% of resources, both in person time
and also in healthcare funding.
And at the moment, they're the people getting a very raw deal
from the system.
The National Health and Performance Authority last year said
that these sort of patients are being seen over 20 times in general practice and often
are seeing more than five GPs in a year. And for someone with very complex healthcare needs,
as Beth described, that's very dangerous. So trying to look at strengthening the business
model for general practice, providing a lot more holistic, ongoing, continuous care is the challenge
that has been discussed over the last two years.
And the healthcare home trials that will start next year
will try and build our understanding of what that might look like,
what Australian patients would like to see in that relationship,
what sort of opportunities that offers,
and what sort of checks and balances that would need.
So this is where you would voluntarily,
as in the UK where you register with a GP,
in the healthcare home you would voluntarily register
with a GP of your choice.
So in 65,000 Australians in 200 practices across the year will be invited to participate
in this new model of care. It'll be entirely voluntary, only for patients with really complex
chronic conditions. They will enroll in a practice, which means the practice will offer them a
nominated clinician. One would imagine that would be their general practitioner who's aware of their
problems and priorities and their wishes and is responsible for all the coordination of their care
within the practice team, but also more generally within the hospital and wider team.
Patients will have access to that clinician and their team, not just face-to-face, which is the
way the Medicare rebate recognises it now, but via email, potentially via video conference,
via phone. That's based around agreements reached between the patient and their family and the
practice. And that the hope is that patients and their family and carers will become much more
partners in their care, that they will build a lot more self-management skills, that they will
manage their own health and be supported in a variety of ways to really build their confidence
about managing healthcare themselves.
How does it solve Beth Oliver's problem?
Is she going to get more pay out of it?
So the funding model will change to support that.
So instead of Beth needing to see someone
sitting beside her in her practice
to actually receive remuneration
and for the patient to receive a Medicare rebate,
the practice and practitioner will receive a monthly,
what is called a bundled payment
to recognise the costs to that practice of extending that support to patients outside face-to-face.
That is going to be really the focus of the trial,
looking at how non-face-to-face care can really offer benefits to patients and their families
and be managed within the practice in contemporary manner.
We use online banking, we use online shopping,
but unfortunately our Medicare rebates are limited to a face-to-face encounter.
This will open that up to what is hoped a lot of innovation between patients and their practices
around how they can best meet the needs they have outside that face-to-face encounter,
which Beth is describing.
Claire, thanks for joining us.
Thank you very much for having me, Norman. Always a pleasure.
Claire Jackson is Professor of General Practice at the University of Queensland
and you're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
I'm Norman Swan.
The lung function of a young baby can predict the persistence of asthma in young adults
and in kids who develop asthma, their lung function soon after birth can help to find out those whose asthma will resolve before adulthood.
This is all according to pioneering Western Australian research, which has now been going on for nearly 25 years
and may tell us a lot about the importance of pregnancy for lung development.
The Health Report covered the study in its early days,
and now they're reporting on the babies who've grown up to be grown-ups.
To tell us more is the lead author and paediatric respiratory physician, Louisa Owens.
Thanks for joining us, Louisa.
Thanks for having me, Norman.
When you talk about infant lung function, what are we actually talking about here?
Well, there's a number of different tests that you can do in infancy for small babies,
and these have evolved over the last number of years.
So actually, the tests that we did back in the late 80s in this study
have changed quite considerably or evolved, I guess, to what we do now.
But we're trying to mimic the lung function tests that older children and adults can do
so that it's something that we can follow longitudinally to see how it changes with time.
So mimicking how much you can blow out in a second, that sort of thing.
Exactly, yeah.
So with small babies, we have to sedate them so that they're asleep
because we need to measure their breathing while they're relaxed.
And we use different manoeuvres so we can put a jacket around their chest,
which we put a balloon inside and inflate the balloon
and that causes them to breathe out forcefully and we measure that flow.
We can also get them to breathe the gas
and see how long it takes them to breathe the gas out
to see how much blockage there is in the airways.
So once you've measured that, at what age?
So we can do it from birth.
It's been done even in preterm infants.
But really from about two months of age, they need to be sedated.
Before that, you can do it just in gentle sleep.
So the findings that you've made have been related to babies
who have reduced lung function at birth and then following them through.
Exactly.
So this was based on the Perth Infant Asthma Follow-Up Study,
which was initiated by Professors Lou Landau and Peter LeSwift.
And they initially recruited a normal cohort from an antenatal hospital in Perth.
So mothers who were pregnant were recruited onto the study
and their infants were then tested during infancy.
Their lung function was tested and they've been followed up.
They're now 24 to 26 years old and we're still looking at their lung function
to see how it's evolved right throughout childhood and adolescence.
So tell me what you found in the 25-year-olds or the 24-year-olds.
Well, when we were specifically looking at those who had asthma,
so the 24-year-olds, the young adults who had asthma,
we were able to look back and see that their lung function
had been significantly lower in infancy at just one month of age.
So shortly after birth, their lung function was already reduced,
suggesting that their asthma was really due to in utero development.
So they had smaller airways?
Smaller airways, yeah, which can be related to the size of the infant.
So we corrected for the size of the infant and found that they had smaller airways and lower flow.
I guess they were breathing out slower than those who didn't have asthma at 24 years of age.
And it was a very significant difference that we could see.
And presumably there was variation amongst that.
It wasn't one and one, but it just increased the risk of having asthma as an adult
when you tended to have low infant lung function.
Absolutely.
And one of the limitations of the infant lung function testing
is that there is quite a wide variability.
But when we looked back, there was only 13% of those with asthma at 24
who had normal lung function in infancy.
So it was a significantly smaller number who had lower lung function.
And when they developed asthma in childhood and they had relatively normal lung function in infancy,
they tended to grow out of the asthma, predicted them growing out of the asthma.
Exactly, yes. So those who had asthma during childhood but no symptoms in early adulthood,
they had normal lung function in infancy when we looked back.
Now, in the paper, you've linked this to a smoking-related disease,
which is what we were talking about with Claire and Elizabeth Oliver, Beth Oliver a moment ago,
which is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which is one of the chronic diseases that GPs
look after and people end up in hospital. What's the link here, do you think, with chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease? Well, it's been, we've known that adults with asthma have lower lung function
and it was initially thought to be related to chronic inflammation and recurrent exacerbations
of their asthma, but now we're finding we can link that right back to infancy. So it's more
likely that it's related to in utero development so the next step of our study is to specifically
look at both in utero smoke exposure postnatal smoke exposure and also the genes that affect it
because it appears like as though some babies are more vulnerable to the toxic effects of in utero
smoke exposure so possibly a gene environment interaction so we'll be looking at that
but when i interviewed lou landau about this probably 20 odd years ago he said it was
definitely linked to smoking but you think it's not i mean some mothers who don't smoke do have
babies with reduced infant lung function is that what you're saying so we've we've certainly shown
that smoking is related to reduced lung function in infancy but we haven't yet shown that that
then links to asthma later on so that's what we'll be looking at separately but also following
the lung function to see those who do or don't have asthma and how their in their lung function
right throughout childhood and adolescence is affected by smoking.
So just briefly, because we're running out of time,
apart from not smoking, there's nothing you know yet to tell parents or mothers
to optimise their lung function of their babies at birth?
No, we haven't been able to target specifically what it is
that causes the low lung function.
Certainly in utero smoke exposure has toxic effects.
so we need to look a little bit closer at that to figure out first of all what specifically
in the child makes them more vulnerable to tobacco smoke and then if there's something
that we can do to target that. Louisa thank you. Thank you. Louisa Owens a respiratory physician
who's now at the Sydney Children's Hospital and we'll move on to genes now it's very relevant
follow-through what might be reported related findings a huge international project which
involved a study of people living in the Busselton area of Western Australia, has identified
43 new genetic signals that might indicate a person is up to 3.7 times more likely to
be at risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
That brings the total of known genetic signals to nearly 100.
Professor Alan James is a respiratory physician at Sir Charles Gardner Hospital in Perth and
one of the enormous team involved.
Thank you for making time with us, Alan.
Nice to be here, Norman.
So are these the genes that Louisa was just talking about
that give you an infant with small lungs?
Yes.
The first line in the paper that we're talking about
states that maximally attained lung function
and subsequent decline, excuse me,
all contribute to the risk of developing COPD.
And so we know that events throughout life
contribute to what our lung function is later in life.
And certainly I'd agree that early development in utero development may be a contributing factor to not attaining full lung function.
Now, the study has got a mind-bending name called the Genome-Wide Association Study, a GWAS.
And these are like sort of fishing exercises where you go out hunting and fishing for genes in populations where you know they've got respiratory problems or don't.
I mean, is that a reasonable description of what's somewhat pejorative?
Some people put it in a pejorative way and others...
Stamp collecting is what some people call it, yeah.
And others look upon it more optimistically.
We know from populations, looking at populations like Busselton and other population studies of lung function,
that we can, by studying family members and unrelated members,
that about 40% of lung function is probably related to inherited factors,
including genes and epigenetic effects.
Just hold on a second.
The epigenetic effects are where the gene itself is not mutated,
but something happens around the outside to change its shape
and the way it interacts with proteins and so on.
And it's kind of, literally what it means is an on-the-outside phenomenon
rather than on the inside with DNA.
That's right.
Something that can determine whether the gene is turned off or on
that arises in the environment but then is inherited by offspring.
And so 40% of these effects seem to be important
in determining our lung function.
And what this large fishing expedition has shown
that we've uncovered up to about 10% of those genes now
using these very large studies of sites on the genome
that are likely to be affecting lung function.
And so coming back to the conversation with Lisa,
are these genes that interact with smoking
or are they genes that knacker your lungs no matter what?
Well, interestingly, only one gene of the 43 new genes
or new sites that were discovered seems to be related to smoking.
Most of the functional genes or genes, sorry, most of the signals that were related to identified genes
seem to be related to inflammation, lung structure, and smooth muscle,
all of which affect airway and lung function.
So not much related to smoking.
Is it related to asthma?
and these may be relevant to asthma of course which is related again to your lung function
again we don't have a lot of time but when you i mean one of the problems with
gene-wide association studies is each individual genetic signal is often incredibly rare
to what extent are you you know somebody's listening they've got asthma or the chronic
lung disease are these genes relevant to them well this is what we're finding more and more
we have to look at large numbers because it's probable that the genetic effects
of lung function may vary from family to family so that families are unalike and that not just
one single gene or a few handfuls of genes determines lung function across the whole
population. But you think you've found genes that might be potential drug targets?
Yes, there was two or three genes related to what we call the acetylcholine receptor.
Acetylcholine is a chemical that determines neural function and its transmission to muscle.
And there are already drugs that we're using to treat asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease.
and it may be that finding genes like this
can help us identify people
who are going to benefit most
from those sorts of treatments
and provide goals for new treatments.
Alan, thanks for joining us.
It's a pleasure, Norman.
Alan James, Professor Alan James,
who's a respiratory physician
at Charles Garner Hospital in Perth
and you're listening to the Health Board,
which indeed is coming today from Perth.
Let's leave the lungs for our sleep and jet lag
because since WA steadfastly clings to the belief
that daylight saving fades the curtains.
There's a three-hour gap with the East,
apart from Queensland,
where they still believe
that daylight savings fades the curtains.
So I'm coming to you at nearly 3 p.m. Western time.
Ian Dunnegan of UWA's Centre for Sleep Science
is studying sleep and jet lag,
and his subjects are the Western Force,
WA's super rugby franchise,
who have to travel a lot for their fixtures.
Welcome to the health report, Ian.
So is there a problem with Western Force?
Well, there's not such a problem with Western Force,
but they do provide a unique opportunity
for us to investigate the effect of jet lag on performance, cognitive and physical, within the
Super Rugby competition. So they're flying all over the place? Yeah. It's not just the three-hour
lag to the east? No, for sure. They're the most traveled sports team in the world. They travel to
South Africa, Japan, New Zealand, to the east coast of Australia. And now in this year, they will be
traveling to Argentina for the first time ever. So how are you studying them? So we're using a range
of different methods over the past few years with the Western Force. But more specifically this year,
we are using biomathematical modelling, which allows us to determine the cognitive performance
effectiveness of the players individually and at a team level. And this is done by a range of
different factors, including the use of wrist activity monitors from a company called Fatigue
Science. And what do you find? Well, we're finding that on average, athletes are sleeping just a
little bit short of seven hours a night, which is not optimal. And indeed, recent sleep health...
More than I get. Probably more than you get too.
Indeed, recent Sleep Health Foundation statistics showed adults are getting around seven hours.
So athletes are no different.
You're also finding that they are sleep banking.
In other words, they're sleeping more before matches, which is what people say you shouldn't do.
There's no advantage to banking up your sleep.
Well, in the general population, we do try to encourage people to have a routine around sleep.
But with professional athletes, it's not so easy with travel, training and so on.
So athletes on the night before the game in this environment
seem to tend to bank sleep or optimize sleep the night before
to get through those periods.
And does that improve their cognitive score?
It does.
It drives up the cognitive score for before the game and during the game.
Because cognitive scores really, I mean,
I think one of your statistics is that 77% is the same
as having a 0.05 level of alcohol in your blood.
Indeed.
And that can equate as well to a reduction in reaction time,
sorry, an increase in reaction time by 34%.
So basically they're getting worse.
And the use of caffeine?
Yeah, so caffeine has been widely used across athletes.
And that's legal?
It is legal, yeah.
And what's that doing to them?
Screwing them up or giving them better performance or what?
So many athletes take caffeine for ergogenic performance
for during the game.
However, the negative...
So to generate energy.
Yeah.
But the negative effect is post-game
from the timing of the caffeine
affects the time of sleep onset.
So in a general population, we see the same thing.
Caffeine full life and half-life.
The caffeine half-life being between four and six hours can actually stop people falling asleep.
So you've retimed when they take the caffeine for the benefit during the match.
Yes, for sure.
So what have you learned?
I mean, if it works for athletes, sleep banking, for example, surely it's going to work for us.
So what have you learned for the common regard to non-rugby player here?
So we see sleep banking or sleep optimisation being utilised in other areas as well, such as military.
but for people who may not be getting sufficient sleep,
such as shift workers,
particularly here in Western Australia
and the mining oil and gas industry,
sleep banking or sleep optimisation
can indeed help for recovery
after periods of sleep loss.
Ideally, the general routine and sleep hygiene
is the best way to go
but if you do know you're going to come up
to periods of sleep loss,
sleep banking can indeed help people
to override those negative cognitive effects.
So adolescent males know something here?
Well, more recently we found
where elite athletes at the AIS,
that young athletes and teenagers
have a delayed chronotype,
so they like to go to bed later and sleep in.
So that's just their normal circadian physiology,
so have an evening chronotype.
And caffeine, obviously,
we kind of know that already earlier in the day
rather than later.
Yeah, for sure.
We see this in the general population and with athletes.
We tend to advise athletes not to have caffeine habitually
after two o'clock in the afternoon,
same with general population.
and even before matches,
if we can avoid caffeine for 24 to 48 hours,
we can get a better ergogenic effect
from the caffeine prior to the game.
So if you deposit some sleep in the bank,
don't remove it with some caffeine.
Exactly.
Thank you very much, Ian Dunnegan,
who's at the University of Western Australia
Centre for Sleep Science.
I'm Norman Swan.
This has been The Health Report.
See you next week.
